title: Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation: Don’t Ignore High-Confidence Student Tokens

paper.title: Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation: Don’t Ignore High-Confidence Student Tokens
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own trajectories using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher.
We show that standard sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, such that their weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply weak or uninformative teacher supervision.
We introduce Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD) , which directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token.
This yields a bounded probability space correction that preserves teacher–student disagreement while avoiding the additional confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla OPD.
Fixed-rollout analyses show that Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher–student disagreement.
We further analyze the resulting model behavior through confidence distributions, answer calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics, showing that Bernoulli OPD’s gains cannot be explained simply by longer reasoning, larger optimization steps, or more uniform imitation of the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/duterscmy/Bernoulli-OPD.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Token distribution and gradient allocation across student-confidence regions. In our primary setting, about 72 % 72\% of sampled tokens are high-confidence with p S > 0.9 p_{S}>0.9 . However, this region receives only about 2.4 % 2.4\% of the total gradient mass under vanilla OPD, compared with about 46.5 % 46.5\% under Bernoulli OPD. The contrast between token frequency and gradient allocation highlights the strong confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla sampled reverse-KL OPD. On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generated trajectories while using a stronger teacher to provide token-level supervision on the visited states ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ) . By learning directly on student-generated trajectories, OPD reduces the distribution mismatch inherent to offline distillation and has shown strong potential for improving language-model reasoning. Despite its effectiveness, the optimization behavior of sampled-token OPD remains poorly understood. In the commonly used sampled reverse-KL objective, the gradient assigned to a sampled token depends not only on teacher–student disagreement, but also strongly on the student’s own confidence. As the student becomes more confident in a sampled token, its gradient is increasingly suppressed, even when the teacher still assigns a meaningfully different probability to that token. This introduces a confidence-dependent bias into how the objective allocates optimization signal. Figure 1 illustrates this effect. High-confidence tokens constitute a large fraction of sampled tokens in student-generated trajectories, yet receive only a small fraction of the total gradient mass under vanilla sampled OPD. Importantly, weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply that these tokens contain little useful teacher supervision. When we train exclusively on highly confident sampled tokens, the student still improves substantially throughout training, although it remains weaker than training on all sampled tokens. This suggests that the limited contribution of high-confidence tokens under vanilla OPD is at least partly induced by the geometry of the objective itself rather than by a lack of useful learning signal. These observations motivate a simple question: can we effectively learn from teacher corrections even when the student is already confident in its prediction? To address this issue, we propose Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD) . Instead of using the sampled reverse-KL log ratio objective, Bernoulli OPD treats each sampled token as a simple binary prediction and directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token. This gives a bounded update that follows the difference between the teacher and student probabilities, without further weakening the training signal on high-confidence tokens. Our experiments support both the proposed mechanism and its practical utility. On identical student rollouts, Bernoulli OPD allocates substantially more optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher–student disagreement. In our primary setting, Bernoulli OPD improves the five-benchmark average from 44.38 to 51.76 over vanilla OPD, and this advantage is reproduced across three independent training seeds (Appendix D ). More broadly, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves over vanilla OPD across four teacher–student settings, covering both Qwen3 and DeepSeek-based students, different types of teacher models, and both non-thinking and thinking generation modes.

sections.heading: Our contributions are summarized as follows.
sections.text: • We show that sampled reverse-KL OPD gives very little optimization signal to high-confidence tokens, even though these tokens are common in student rollouts and can still provide useful learning signal. • We propose Bernoulli OPD, a simple objective that directly matches teacher and student token probabilities and avoids unnecessarily weakening updates on high-confidence tokens. • Across four teacher–student settings, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves reasoning performance over vanilla OPD. We further analyze its behavior through confidence distributions, answer-level calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics.

sections.heading: Off-policy and on-policy distillation.
sections.text: Classical knowledge distillation learns from a fixed data distribution ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence-level distillation often uses teacher-generated responses ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . On-policy distillation instead trains on student generated trajectories, reducing the mismatch between training and inference states ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . Existing OPD methods can be broadly divided into full vocabulary ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , Top- k k ( Meng et al., 2026 ) , and sampled token variants ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Full vocabulary methods use dense teacher distributions, Top- k k methods retain only a restricted support, and sampled-based methods use student sampled tokens as Monte Carlo estimates. The latter is particularly attractive for long horizon reasoning research because of its lower memory and communication cost. Our work also focuses on this sampled-token setting.

sections.heading: Sampled-based OPD.
sections.text: Recent work has studied sampled OPD from several perspectives, including teacher–student compatibility, rollout length, sampling, and token-level optimization. OPSA ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) observes that learning under sampled reverse KL is concentrated on low-probability tokens. Building on similar observation, SuRe ( Shao et al., 2026 ) analyzes the underlying gradient structure and further strengthens updates to low-confidence tokens. PowerOPD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) focuses on a different issue, replacing the unbounded log-ratio reward with a bounded transformation to improve training stability. Our work revisits the gradient allocation of sampled OPD from the opposite direction. We ask whether the weak updates assigned to high-confidence tokens are actually justified, and show that these tokens can still provide useful learning signal. This motivates Bernoulli OPD, which directly uses the bounded teacher–student probability difference as its training signal. As a result, high-confidence teacher corrections remain effective without explicitly favoring either low- or high-confidence tokens.

sections.heading: Binary objectives in computer vision distillation.
sections.text: Binary formulations have been explored in computer vision distillation. Decoupled Knowledge Distillation (DKD) ( Zhao et al., 2022 ) separates the target class from the remaining classes in image classification. Related binary formulations have also been used to distill class predictions in object detection ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Bernoulli OPD uses a related binary view in a different setting. For each student-sampled token, we group the vocabulary into the sampled token and its complement, and match the corresponding teacher and student Bernoulli probabilities. Our goal is not to separate class-level knowledge, but to preserve useful teacher corrections on high-confidence tokens that receive weak gradients under sampled reverse KL.

sections.heading: High-confidence tokens dominate rollouts but receive weak gradients.
sections.text: This confidence-dependent suppression is substantial in practice. As shown in Figure 1 , more than 70 % 70\% of sampled tokens lie in the highest-confidence region p S ∈ [ 0.9 , 1.0 ) p_{\mathrm{S}}\in[0.9,1.0) . Despite dominating the rollout distribution, these tokens have much smaller per-token gradients and consequently account for only a limited share of the total gradient mass. Optimization under vanilla sampled OPD is therefore distributed very differently from the sampled-token distribution itself. Importantly, this imbalance does not by itself imply that high-confidence tokens are uninformative. A small gradient can arise either because the teacher and student already agree, or because the objective suppresses the gradient when the student is highly confident. Distinguishing these two cases is important for understanding whether the gradient allocation of vanilla OPD is desirable. Figure 2 : Training with high-confidence sampled tokens. This diagnostic experiment uses our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting. Vanilla OPD restricted to tokens with p S > 0.9 p_{\mathrm{S}}>0.9 still yields substantial performance gains despite the strong gradient suppression in this confidence region.

sections.heading: High-confidence tokens can still provide useful training signal.
sections.text: To test whether the high-confidence region contains useful learning signal, we train Vanilla OPD using only sampled tokens with p S > 0.9 p_{\mathrm{S}}>0.9 . Figure 2 shows that the student continues to improve substantially throughout training despite discarding all lower-confidence tokens. High-confidence tokens are therefore not devoid of useful teacher supervision, even though vanilla OPD assigns them relatively little gradient mass. Together, these results reveal a mismatch between token informativeness and objective-induced gradient allocation. High-confidence tokens are both abundant and learnable, yet their updates are systematically attenuated by the confidence dependence of sampled reverse KL. This motivates an objective that preserves teacher–student disagreement as a learning signal without additionally suppressing updates merely because the student is already confident.

For each sampled token y t y_{t} , consider the binary event B t = 𝟙 [ Y = y t ] . B_{t}=\mathbb{1}[Y=y_{t}]. sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: We evaluate four teacher--student configurations spanning two student models. For Qwen3-1.7B, we use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/pb09204048/Qwen3-8B-DAPO-iter449-disable-thinking as teachers, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as our primary setting ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, we use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Skywork-OR1-Math-7B as teachers. Following the native generation conventions of the corresponding model families, we evaluate the Qwen3 settings in non-thinking mode and the DeepSeek-based settings in thinking mode. Training prompts are drawn from DAPO-Math-17K ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Within each teacher–student setting, all methods share the same student initialization, rollout prompts, generation mode, and optimization configuration; only the distillation objective changes, unless otherwise specified. Full training and implementation details are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate checkpoints on AIME24 ( Jia, 2024 ) and select the best checkpoint using Avg@ 8 8 . Final evaluation covers AIME24, AIME25 ( math-ai, 2025 ) , HMMT25 ( Balunović et al., 2026 ) , AMC23 ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , and MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) . The first four benchmarks are reported with Avg@ 32 32 , while MATH500 uses Avg@ 4 4 . Decoding parameters and evaluation details are given in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Baselines and variants.
sections.text: We compare against vanilla sampled reverse-KL OPD, SuRe ( Shao et al., 2026 ) , and PowerOPD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We implement SuRe within our framework and evaluate it under the same unified training setup as our methods. For PowerOPD, we evaluate both the unified and official reference configurations and report the better result for each teacher–student setting to ensure a fair and conservative comparison. Implementation details and results for both configurations are provided in Appendix A.4 . Among our methods, GC-OPD serves as a diagnostic control that removes the explicit 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} suppression while retaining the log-ratio signal, whereas Bernoulli OPD is our primary proposed objective. We additionally study Balanced Bernoulli OPD and a scale-matched Bernoulli control in Section 5.3 to examine confidence-level rebalancing and the effect of overall optimization magnitude.

sections.heading: 5.2 Main Results
sections.text: Table 2 summarizes the main results across four teacher–student settings. Bernoulli OPD improves aggregate reasoning performance over vanilla OPD in all four settings, with gains ranging from 0.98 0.98 to 7.38 7.38 points. The largest improvement occurs in our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting, where Bernoulli OPD increases the five-benchmark average from 44.38 44.38 to 51.76 51.76 . The improvement also persists with the Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL teacher and across both settings using the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B student, indicating that the benefit is not specific to a single student or teacher family. The existing baselines show different strengths across settings. SuRe modifies the confidence preference of sampled OPD, while PowerOPD uses a bounded transformation of the log-ratio reward and provides a strong competitive baseline. Bernoulli OPD achieves the highest aggregate performance across all four settings. GC-OPD also improves over vanilla OPD in every setting, providing evidence that reducing the confidence-dependent suppression of sampled reverse KL can be beneficial. Bernoulli OPD further improves over GC-OPD across all four settings. One possible explanation is that Bernoulli OPD not only removes the additional suppression of high-confidence tokens, but also expresses teacher–student disagreement directly through a Bernoulli cross-entropy objective with a bounded sampled-token logit gradient. This combination may provide a more effective training signal across different teacher–student settings. The magnitude of the Bernoulli OPD improvement nevertheless varies substantially across teachers. This suggests that correcting gradient allocation determines which teacher corrections can act strongly on the student, but does not by itself determine how useful those corrections are. We further analyze this teacher-dependent variation in Sec. 5.4 . Figure 4 : Confidence redistribution after OPD training. Changes in token share across confidence bins relative to the initial student under (a) fixed-rollout rescoring and (b) on-policy generation. Bernoulli OPD shows the strongest redistribution away from the highest-confidence region.

sections.heading: 5.3 Additional Variants for Bernoulli OPD
sections.text: We further examine two questions: (1) does making the gradient allocation more uniform across confidence regions improve performance? (2) are the gains of Bernoulli OPD simply due to a larger overall optimization step?

sections.heading: Balanced Bernoulli OPD.
sections.text: Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens, but it does not explicitly attempt to equalize gradient mass across confidence regions. Its gradient magnitude remains determined by the underlying teacher–student probability discrepancy, | p S − p T | |p_{S}-p_{T}| , which can itself vary substantially with student confidence. sections.heading: Gradient-scale control.
sections.text: Figure 3 shows that Bernoulli OPD produces a substantially different gradient profile from vanilla OPD, raising the possibility that its gain results simply from a larger overall update. To isolate this effect, we construct a scale-matched Bernoulli variant whose loss is rescaled at initialization to match the full-model gradient norm of vanilla OPD. Table 4 summarizes the result. Scale matching makes both the initial gradient norm and one-step policy movement nearly identical to vanilla OPD while preserving Bernoulli OPD’s distinct confidence-dependent gradient allocation. The downstream advantage also remains: scale-matched Bernoulli reaches an average accuracy of 52.58 52.58 , compared with 44.38 44.38 for vanilla OPD and 51.76 51.76 for standard Bernoulli OPD. In this diagnostic setting, the gain therefore cannot be explained solely by a larger global update. We use scale matching only as a diagnostic control because it requires calibration against vanilla OPD. Full calibration details are provided in Appendix C . Table 4 : Gradient-scale control. sections.heading: 5.4 Teacher-Dependent Variation
sections.text: The benefit of Bernoulli OPD varies substantially across teacher–student settings. In our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting, Bernoulli OPD improves the five-benchmark average over vanilla OPD by 7.38 7.38 points, whereas the gain with Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL is only 1.02 1.02 points. The two DeepSeek-based settings also show different gains, ranging from 0.98 0.98 to 2.08 2.08 points. These results suggest that teacher strength or student–teacher performance headroom alone does not determine how much Bernoulli OPD benefits from the teacher signal. To investigate this difference, we score exactly the same Qwen3-1.7B student rollouts with the 4B-Instruct and 8B-DAPO teachers. Both exhibit nearly the same confidence-dependent imbalance under vanilla OPD: more than 90 % 90\% of sampled tokens lie in the highest-confidence region, yet this region receives only about 3 % 3\% of the vanilla gradient-proxy mass. Bernoulli OPD restores this contribution to approximately 47 47 – 49 % 49\% for both teachers. Thus, the existence of high-confidence suppression alone is also insufficient to predict the downstream gain. Our additional analysis suggests that the quality of the recovered correction may matter in addition to its magnitude. The 4B-Instruct teacher provides slightly more outcome-aligned Bernoulli signals on the fixed rollouts, although the statistical difference is not conclusive. One possible factor is teacher provenance: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is a newer instruction-tuned checkpoint and may differ substantially in supervised post-training, whereas Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL is obtained by further RL training a model from the same Qwen3 base generation as the student. Such differences may affect the compatibility and teachability of teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. We provide the detailed signal analysis in Appendix B . sections.heading: Confidence redistribution.
sections.text: We next examine how different OPD objectives affect the confidence distribution of the trained student. Figure 4 reports the change in token share across confidence bins relative to the initial student. Under fixed-rollout rescoring, where all models are evaluated on the same prefixes and target tokens, Bernoulli OPD produces the largest redistribution away from the highest-confidence region. GC-OPD shows a similar but weaker trend, while Vanilla OPD, SuRe, and PowerOPD induce substantially smaller changes. Because the evaluated states and tokens are fixed, this effect cannot be explained solely by differences in generated trajectories. The same pattern becomes even more pronounced under on-policy generation. Bernoulli OPD substantially reduces the concentration of tokens in the p S ∈ [ 0.9 , 1.0 ] p_{S}\in[0.9,1.0] bin and redistributes probability mass toward lower confidence regions. Together, these results suggest that the different gradient allocation of Bernoulli OPD leads to a measurable change in the confidence behavior of the trained model. Importantly, restoring gradients to high-confidence tokens does not imply increasing their confidence: teacher corrections can instead reduce excessively confident predictions, consistent with the redistribution observed here.

sections.heading: Answer-level calibration.
sections.text: We next examine whether the changes in confidence induced by different objectives translate into meaningful uncertainty at the answer level. On MATH500, we sample 8 responses per problem and define the confidence of the predicted answer as the fraction of samples belonging to its majority answer cluster. Figure 5 compares each method with Vanilla OPD in terms of majority-answer accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Bernoulli OPD exhibits the most favorable point-estimate trade-off, suggesting that Bernoulli OPD’s confidence redistribution does not come at the expense of answer-level calibration; instead, it is accompanied by both higher answer consistency accuracy and lower calibration error.

sections.heading: Policy movement.
sections.text: We further examine whether the improvements from Bernoulli OPD can be explained by globally imitating the teacher’s next-token distribution. Figure 6 measures policy movement on fixed Base rollouts across two teacher–student settings. We compare the drift from the initial student policy with the corresponding change in Top-20 vocabulary overlap with the teacher. Across both settings, Bernoulli OPD substantially changes the student policy without a comparable increase in global teacher overlap. In contrast, Vanilla OPD and SuRe exhibit stronger increases in teacher overlap despite achieving weaker downstream performance. These results suggest that Bernoulli OPD’s gains do not require a corresponding increase in Top-20 vocabulary overlap with the teacher.

sections.heading: Training dynamics.
sections.text: We finally examine how accuracy and generation length evolve during training in our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting. Figure 7 compares Vanilla OPD, GC-OPD, and Bernoulli OPD on AIME24 using the same evaluation protocol. All three methods exhibit a sharp but transient increase in response length early in training, accompanied by a substantial rise in truncation rate. Response length and truncation then steadily decrease as training continues. Importantly, accuracy does not simply track response length. Bernoulli OPD maintains higher AIME24 validation accuracy over most later checkpoints even after its response length and truncation rate have fallen substantially. This suggests that its performance gain cannot be explained solely by generating longer responses, but reflects a different learning trajectory induced by the objective.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, even though these tokens can still provide useful learning signal. We introduce Bernoulli OPD, which replaces the log-ratio surrogate with a Bernoulli cross-entropy objective whose sampled-token logit gradient directly reflects the bounded teacher–student probability difference. Across four teacher–student settings, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves over vanilla OPD. Our controls further show that the gain is not explained simply by a larger update or by enforcing more uniform gradients across confidence regions. Overall, our results highlight the importance of separating token informativeness from the gradient geometry of the distillation objective.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This work improves the efficiency of transferring mathematical reasoning to smaller language models. While effective distillation can reduce deployment costs, it may also propagate teacher errors or undesirable behavior. Our analysis helps interpret such transfer, and all experiments use public mathematical datasets without sensitive data.

sections.heading: A.1 Training Setup
sections.text: Unless otherwise specified, the following training settings apply to our unified experiments. All experiments are conducted on four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. Two GPUs are used for actor training, while the remaining two are used for rollout generation and teacher inference. Training prompts are sampled from DAPO-Math-17K. For the Qwen3-1.7B settings, generation is performed in non-thinking mode. For the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B settings, we retain the default thinking behavior of the reasoning models. For each prompt, we generate one student response at temperature 1.0 1.0 with a maximum generation length of 12,000 12{,}000 tokens. Training uses a global batch size of 64 64 and Adam with a constant learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} . Within each teacher–student setting, all compared methods share the same student initialization, rollout prompts, generation configuration, and response masking rules unless otherwise specified. Each method generates its own on-policy trajectories and obtains teacher scores on the corresponding student-generated tokens. The unified experiments additionally share the same loss normalization, optimizer, and training schedule. PowerOPD results using its reference training recipe are described separately in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: A.2 Evaluation and Checkpoint Selection
sections.text: We evaluate checkpoints every 20 20 training updates on AIME24. Checkpoint selection uses Avg@ 8 8 with temperature 0.7 0.7 , top- p p 0.8 0.8 , top- k k 20 20 , and a maximum response length of 32,768 32{,}768 tokens. The selected checkpoint is the one with the highest AIME24 Avg@ 8 8 . Final evaluation uses the same decoding parameters. We report Avg@ 32 32 on AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, and AMC23, and Avg@ 4 4 on MATH500. For the Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL teacher setting, the maximum response length is increased to 38,912 38{,}912 tokens because the resulting student generations are substantially longer. Final-answer accuracy is computed using the same mathematical answer extraction and grading pipeline across all methods.

sections.text: For Balanced Bernoulli OPD, valid response tokens are partitioned into 10 10 student-confidence bins. We use β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 and clip the normalized detached bin weights to [ 1 / 5 , 5 ] [1/5,5] . The weighting coefficients are computed from aggregate Bernoulli gradient mass within each confidence bin, as defined in Section 5.3 . Balanced Bernoulli OPD is included as an exploratory mechanism control for studying explicit confidence-level rebalancing rather than as a fully tuned primary method.

sections.heading: A.5 Answer-Level Calibration Details
sections.text: For the answer-level calibration analysis in Section 5.5 , we sample eight responses per MATH500 problem. We extract and normalize the final mathematical answer from each response and cluster answers by mathematical equivalence using exact matching together with the MathD and SymPy graders. Responses for which no valid answer can be extracted are assigned to a single INVALID cluster. The largest answer cluster is treated as the model prediction, and its relative frequency among the eight samples defines the answer-level confidence. If multiple clusters are tied for the largest size, we select the cluster containing the earliest generated response. We compute Expected Calibration Error (ECE) using 10 equal-width bins over [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] : ECE = ∑ b n b N ​ | conf ⁡ ( b ) − acc ⁡ ( b ) | , \mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b}\frac{n_{b}}{N}\left|\mathrm{conf}(b)-\mathrm{acc}(b)\right|, (18) where n b n_{b} is the number of problems in bin b b , and conf ⁡ ( b ) \mathrm{conf}(b) and acc ⁡ ( b ) \mathrm{acc}(b) denote its mean answer-level confidence and empirical accuracy, respectively. Because each problem has eight samples, the confidence values are restricted to multiples of 1 / 8 1/8 . This quantity should be interpreted as sampling-based answer consistency rather than the model’s exact probability assigned to the correct answer.

The resulting implementation is ℒ Bern = − p ~ T ​ log ⁡ p S − ( 1 − p ~ T ) ​ log1p ⁡ ( − p ~ S ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Bern}}=-\tilde{p}_{T}\log p_{S}-(1-\tilde{p}_{T})\operatorname{log1p}(-\tilde{p}_{S}), where p ~ T \tilde{p}_{T} is the clipped, detached teacher probability. sections.heading: B.2 Outcome Alignment of Teacher Corrections
sections.text: We next ask whether the teacher corrections emphasized by Bernoulli OPD are related to rollout quality. We evaluate both teachers on the same 120 fixed Base rollouts from AIME24, containing 17 correct and 103 incorrect responses. For each response i i , we define a sequence-level Bernoulli correction score as s i ( T ) = 1 | ℳ i | ​ ∑ t ∈ ℳ i [ p T ​ ( y i , t ∣ c i , t ) − p S ​ ( y i , t ∣ c i , t ) ] , s_{i}^{(T)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\left[p_{T}(y_{i,t}\mid c_{i,t})-p_{S}(y_{i,t}\mid c_{i,t})\right], (19) where ℳ i \mathcal{M}_{i} contains valid response-token positions after applying the loss mask and excluding special tokens. Both teachers are evaluated on the same student-generated tokens using teacher-forced scoring. The score averages signed probability differences over valid tokens, including the observed tokens of truncated responses. We measure how well this score distinguishes correct from incorrect responses using AUROC, with rollout correctness as the positive label. The resulting AUROC is 0.704 0.704 for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and 0.690 0.690 for Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL. Although the difference is small, the numerically higher AUROC for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is consistent with its larger downstream gain. We do not draw a strong conclusion about teacher differences from this diagnostic alone.

sections.heading: B.3 Interpretation
sections.text: These results point to two separate factors. The loss determines how much of the available teacher signal can affect the student, while the teacher determines how useful that signal is. Bernoulli OPD reduces the suppression of high-confidence corrections, but the final gain still depends on the quality of the teacher feedback on the states visited by the student. One possible explanation lies in the different model origins and training histories of the teachers. Although Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL undergoes additional reinforcement learning, its base model, Qwen3-8B, belongs to the same model generation as the Qwen3-1.7B student. In contrast, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 comes from a different Qwen3 generation with a potentially different pretraining and post-training history. These differences may affect the nature and usefulness of teacher corrections on student-generated trajectories. A full explanation of this teacher-dependent effect is left for future work.

sections.heading: C.2 One-Step Optimization Calibration
sections.text: Matching the raw gradient norm does not necessarily imply a matched optimizer update, particularly under Adam. We therefore additionally measure the one-step change in the student policy after applying the optimizer update. Specifically, starting from the same student parameters, we apply one optimizer step and measure the mean absolute change in sampled-token log probability, M = 𝔼 t ​ [ | log ⁡ p θ + ​ ( y t ∣ c t ) − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( y t ∣ c t ) | ] , M=\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\left|\log p_{\theta^{+}}(y_{t}\mid c_{t})-\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid c_{t})\right|\right], (22) where θ \theta and θ + \theta^{+} denote the parameters before and after the update. As reported in Table 4 , scale matching makes both the full-model gradient norm and the resulting one-step policy movement nearly identical to vanilla OPD. At the same time, the high-confidence region retains the substantially larger share of gradient mass induced by the Bernoulli objective. Thus, the control matches global optimization magnitude without removing the confidence-dependent redistribution that distinguishes Bernoulli OPD.

sections.heading: C.3 Training the Scale-Matched Variant
sections.text: We train the scale-matched variant in the primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting. The coefficient c = 0.8145 c=0.8145 is fixed throughout training, with no per-step normalization or other change to the optimization configuration. Checkpoint selection follows the same AIME24 Avg@ 8 8 protocol as the main experiments. Table 4 shows that matching the global update scale does not remove the downstream advantage of Bernoulli OPD. This rules out a larger initial gradient norm or larger one-step policy movement as the sole explanation for the observed improvement.

sections.heading: C.4 Interpretation
sections.text: The scale-controlled experiment separates the overall magnitude of optimization from its allocation across tokens. After matching vanilla OPD’s global update scale, Bernoulli OPD preserves both its distinct confidence-dependent gradient allocation and its downstream advantage. This supports the interpretation that Bernoulli OPD changes where optimization is allocated rather than merely increasing how much optimization is applied. Scale-matched Bernoulli slightly outperforms standard Bernoulli OPD in this run. We do not interpret this difference as evidence that scale matching is systematically beneficial, since the experiment uses a single training seed and requires an additional calibration step. We therefore treat scale matching strictly as a mechanism control rather than as a proposed training method.

sections.heading: D.1 Experimental Protocol
sections.text: We additionally evaluate the robustness of our primary comparison to training randomness. In the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting, we repeat both Vanilla OPD and Bernoulli OPD with three independent training seeds. For reference, we also evaluate the initial Qwen3-1.7B student three times using independent stochastic decoding runs. For every trained model, checkpoint selection is performed independently using the same AIME24 Avg@ 8 8 protocol as in the main experiments. The first four final-evaluation benchmarks use Avg@32, while MATH500 uses Avg@4.

sections.heading: D.2 Results
sections.text: Table 8 shows that both Vanilla OPD and Bernoulli OPD exhibit small run-to-run variation. The five-benchmark average of Vanilla OPD is 44.44 ± 0.16 44.44\pm 0.16 , whereas Bernoulli OPD achieves 51.62 ± 0.18 51.62\pm 0.18 . The approximately seven-point improvement of Bernoulli OPD is therefore substantially larger than the observed training-seed variation and is reproduced consistently across all three independent training runs. The individual benchmark results are also broadly consistent across training seeds. In addition, final evaluation averages multiple stochastic generations per problem, which reduces variance from stochastic decoding. Given the computational cost of repeating every combination of method and teacher, and the small training-seed variability observed in this controlled primary comparison, we report a single training run for the remaining experiments unless otherwise stated.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.02093v1 [cs.LG] 01 Nov 2026 Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation: Don’t Ignore High-Confidence Student Tokens Mingyu Cao Affiliation: University of Surrey Yaokai Jin Affiliation: University College London Shiwei Liu Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems Affiliation: Tübingen AI Center Lu Yin Affiliation: University of Surrey Correspondence to: l.yin@surrey.ac.uk Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own trajectories using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher. We show that standard sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, such that their weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply weak or uninformative teacher supervision. We introduce Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD) , which directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token. This yields a bounded probability space correction that preserves teacher–student disagreement while avoiding the additional confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla OPD. Fixed-rollout analyses show that Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher–student disagreement. We further analyze the resulting model behavior through confidence distributions, answer calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics, showing that Bernoulli OPD’s gains cannot be explained simply by longer reasoning, larger optimization steps, or more uniform imitation of the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/duterscmy/Bernoulli-OPD. Keywords: on-policy distillation, knowledge distillation, language models, optimization geometry 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Token distribution and gradient allocation across student-confidence regions. In our primary setting, about 72 % 72\% of sampled tokens are high-confidence with p S > 0.9 p_{S}>0.9 . However, this region receives only about 2.4 % 2.4\% of the total gradient mass under vanilla OPD, compared with about 46.5 % 46.5\% under Bernoulli OPD. The contrast between token frequency and gradient allocation highlights the strong confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla sampled reverse-KL OPD. On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generated trajectories while using a stronger teacher to provide token-level supervision on the visited states ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ) . By learning directly on student-generated trajectories, OPD reduces the distribution mismatch inherent to offline distillation and has shown strong potential for improving language-model reasoning. Despite its effectiveness, the optimization behavior of sampled-token OPD remains poorly understood. In the commonly used sampled reverse-KL objective, the gradient assigned to a sampled token depends not only on teacher–student disagreement, but also strongly on the student’s own confidence. As the student becomes more confident in a sampled token, its gradient is increasingly suppressed, even when the teacher still assigns a meaningfully different probability to that token. This introduces a confidence-dependent bias into how the objective allocates optimization signal. Figure 1 illustrates this effect. High-confidence tokens constitute a large fraction of sampled tokens in student-generated trajectories, yet receive only a small fraction of the total gradient mass under vanilla sampled OPD. Importantly, weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply that these tokens contain little useful teacher supervision. When we train exclusively on highly confident sampled tokens, the student still improves substantially throughout training, although it remains weaker than training on all sampled tokens. This suggests that the limited contribution of high-confidence tokens under vanilla OPD is at least partly induced by the geometry of the objective itself rather than by a lack of useful learning signal. These observations motivate a simple question: can we effectively learn from teacher corrections even when the student is already confident in its prediction? To address this issue, we propose Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD) . Instead of using the sampled reverse-KL log ratio objective, Bernoulli OPD treats each sampled token as a simple binary prediction and directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token. This gives a bounded update that follows the difference between the teacher and student probabilities, without further weakening the training signal on high-confidence tokens. Our experiments support both the proposed mechanism and its practical utility. On identical student rollouts, Bernoulli OPD allocates substantially more optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher–student disagreement. In our primary setting, Bernoulli OPD improves the five-benchmark average from 44.38 to 51.76 over vanilla OPD, and this advantage is reproduced across three independent training seeds (Appendix D ). More broadly, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves over vanilla OPD across four teacher–student settings, covering both Qwen3 and DeepSeek-based students, different types of teacher models, and both non-thinking and thinking generation modes. Our contributions are summarized as follows. • We show that sampled reverse-KL OPD gives very little optimization signal to high-confidence tokens, even though these tokens are common in student rollouts and can still provide useful learning signal. • We propose Bernoulli OPD, a simple objective that directly matches teacher and student token probabilities and avoids unnecessarily weakening updates on high-confidence tokens. • Across four teacher–student settings, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves reasoning performance over vanilla OPD. We further analyze its behavior through confidence distributions, answer-level calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics. 2 Related Work Off-policy and on-policy distillation. Classical knowledge distillation learns from a fixed data distribution ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence-level distillation often uses teacher-generated responses ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . On-policy distillation instead trains on student generated trajectories, reducing the mismatch between training and inference states ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . Existing OPD methods can be broadly divided into full vocabulary ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , Top- k k ( Meng et al., 2026 ) , and sampled token variants ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Full vocabulary methods use dense teacher distributions, Top- k k methods retain only a restricted support, and sampled-based methods use student sampled tokens as Monte Carlo estimates. The latter is particularly attractive for long horizon reasoning research because of its lower memory and communication cost. Our work also focuses on this sampled-token setting. Sampled-based OPD. Recent work has studied sampled OPD from several perspectives, including teacher–student compatibility, rollout length, sampling, and token-level optimization. OPSA ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) observes that learning under sampled reverse KL is concentrated on low-probability tokens. Building on similar observation, SuRe ( Shao et al., 2026 ) analyzes the underlying gradient structure and further strengthens updates to low-confidence tokens. PowerOPD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) focuses on a different issue, replacing the unbounded log-ratio reward with a bounded transformation to improve training stability. Our work revisits the gradient allocation of sampled OPD from the opposite direction. We ask whether the weak updates assigned to high-confidence tokens are actually justified, and show that these tokens can still provide useful learning signal. This motivates Bernoulli OPD, which directly uses the bounded teacher–student probability difference as its training signal. As a result, high-confidence teacher corrections remain effective without explicitly favoring either low- or high-confidence tokens. Binary objectives in computer vision distillation. Binary formulations have been explored in computer vision distillation. Decoupled Knowledge Distillation (DKD) ( Zhao et al., 2022 ) separates the target class from the remaining classes in image classification. Related binary formulations have also been used to distill class predictions in object detection ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Bernoulli OPD uses a related binary view in a different setting. For each student-sampled token, we group the vocabulary into the sampled token and its complement, and match the corresponding teacher and student Bernoulli probabilities. Our goal is not to separate class-level knowledge, but to preserve useful teacher corrections on high-confidence tokens that receive weak gradients under sampled reverse KL. 3 Background and Motivation Let x x denote a prompt and y 1 : T ∼ p S ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y_{1:T}\sim p_{\mathrm{S}}(\cdot\mid x) a trajectory sampled from the current student. Its gradient contains an additional factor 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} from the softmax geometry. As the student becomes more confident in the sampled token, this factor approaches zero and weakens the corresponding optimization signal. Therefore, even when the teacher still disagrees with a confident student prediction, the token can receive only a small gradient. High-confidence tokens dominate rollouts but receive weak gradients. This confidence-dependent suppression is substantial in practice. As shown in Figure 1 , more than 70 % 70\% of sampled tokens lie in the highest-confidence region p S ∈ [ 0.9 , 1.0 ) p_{\mathrm{S}}\in[0.9,1.0) . Despite dominating the rollout distribution, these tokens have much smaller per-token gradients and consequently account for only a limited share of the total gradient mass. Optimization under vanilla sampled OPD is therefore distributed very differently from the sampled-token distribution itself. Importantly, this imbalance does not by itself imply that high-confidence tokens are uninformative. A small gradient can arise either because the teacher and student already agree, or because the objective suppresses the gradient when the student is highly confident. Distinguishing these two cases is important for understanding whether the gradient allocation of vanilla OPD is desirable. Figure 2 : Training with high-confidence sampled tokens. This diagnostic experiment uses our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting. Vanilla OPD restricted to tokens with p S > 0.9 p_{\mathrm{S}}>0.9 still yields substantial performance gains despite the strong gradient suppression in this confidence region. High-confidence tokens can still provide useful training signal. To test whether the high-confidence region contains useful learning signal, we train Vanilla OPD using only sampled tokens with p S > 0.9 p_{\mathrm{S}}>0.9 . Figure 2 shows that the student continues to improve substantially throughout training despite discarding all lower-confidence tokens. High-confidence tokens are therefore not devoid of useful teacher supervision, even though vanilla OPD assigns them relatively little gradient mass. Together, these results reveal a mismatch between token informativeness and objective-induced gradient allocation. High-confidence tokens are both abundant and learnable, yet their updates are systematically attenuated by the confidence dependence of sampled reverse KL. This motivates an objective that preserves teacher–student disagreement as a learning signal without additionally suppressing updates merely because the student is already confident. 4 Methods Figure 3 : Gradient allocation under different OPD objectives. All methods are evaluated on the same fixed student rollouts. The top row shows the mean per-token gradient proxy across student-confidence bins, and the bottom row shows the corresponding share of total gradient mass . Compared with (a) Vanilla OPD, (b) SuRe further emphasizes low-confidence updates, whereas (c) GC-OPD and (d) Bernoulli OPD substantially restore gradient contribution in high-confidence regions. Top-row y-axis scales differ across objectives; the bottom row reports normalized gradient-mass shares. Vanilla sampled reverse-KL OPD combines teacher–student disagreement with a confidence-dependent factor 1 − p S 1-p_{S} , which strongly suppresses updates on high-confidence sampled tokens. We study this issue through two complementary objectives. GC-OPD removes only the explicit confidence-dependent suppression and serves as a diagnostic control. Our main method, Bernoulli OPD, replaces the sampled log-ratio objective with a Bernoulli cross-entropy objective whose sampled-token logit gradient is bounded. Figure 3 compares their gradient allocation with Vanilla OPD and SuRe on the same fixed student rollouts. 4.1 Geometry-Corrected OPD We first isolate the explicit 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} factor in vanilla OPD while preserving the same teacher–student log-probability signal. Recall A t = log ⁡ p T − log ⁡ p S . A_{t}=\log p_{\mathrm{T}}-\log p_{\mathrm{S}}. (8) GC-OPD therefore removes the explicit 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} suppression of vanilla OPD while retaining the same log-ratio discrepancy. As shown in Figure 3 (c), this substantially restores gradient contribution from high-confidence tokens. We use GC-OPD primarily as a diagnostic control to test whether the confidence-dependent softmax geometry itself limits useful teacher corrections. 4.2 Bernoulli OPD GC-OPD removes the explicit confidence suppression but still relies on the unbounded log-probability gap. We therefore introduce Bernoulli OPD , which instead measures teacher–student disagreement directly in probability space. For each sampled token y t y_{t} , consider the binary event B t = 𝟙 [ Y = y t ] . B_{t}=\mathbb{1}[Y=y_{t}]. (9) The categorical teacher and student distributions induce Bernoulli marginals with parameters p T p_{\mathrm{T}} and p S p_{\mathrm{S}} . We distill these marginals using binary cross-entropy: ℒ Bern , t = − p T ​ log ⁡ p S − ( 1 − p T ) ​ log ⁡ ( 1 − p S ) . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Bern},t}={}&-p_{\mathrm{T}}\log p_{\mathrm{S}}\\ &-(1-p_{\mathrm{T}})\log(1-p_{\mathrm{S}}).\end{split} (10) This objective is a sampled token-versus-complement coarse-graining evaluated at student-visited states, rather than a full-vocabulary forward KL. Its derivative with respect to the sampled-token logit is ∂ ℒ Bern , t ∂ z y = p S − p T . \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Bern},t}}{\partial z_{y}}=p_{\mathrm{S}}-p_{\mathrm{T}}. (11) Bernoulli OPD therefore uses the direct teacher–student probability gap. Unlike vanilla OPD, the correction is not multiplied by an additional vanishing 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} factor. The probability gap is also bounded in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , avoiding the large scale that can arise from log-probability ratios. When teacher and student agree, the update naturally vanishes; when they disagree, the correction remains visible even at high student confidence. This change produces a markedly different gradient allocation. Figure 3 (d) shows that Bernoulli OPD shifts substantial optimization mass toward the high-confidence region that is nearly ignored by vanilla OPD, while still assigning larger per-token updates where teacher–student disagreement is stronger. We evaluate four teacher--student configurations spanning two student models. For Qwen3-1.7B, we use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/pb09204048/Qwen3-8B-DAPO-iter449-disable-thinking as teachers, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as our primary setting ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, we use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Skywork-OR1-Math-7B as teachers. Following the native generation conventions of the corresponding model families, we evaluate the Qwen3 settings in non-thinking mode and the DeepSeek-based settings in thinking mode. Training prompts are drawn from DAPO-Math-17K ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Within each teacher–student setting, all methods share the same student initialization, rollout prompts, generation mode, and optimization configuration; only the distillation objective changes, unless otherwise specified. Full training and implementation details are provided in Appendix A . Evaluation. We evaluate checkpoints on AIME24 ( Jia, 2024 ) and select the best checkpoint using Avg@ 8 8 . Final evaluation covers AIME24, AIME25 ( math-ai, 2025 ) , HMMT25 ( Balunović et al., 2026 ) , AMC23 ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , and MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) . The first four benchmarks are reported with Avg@ 32 32 , while MATH500 uses Avg@ 4 4 . Decoding parameters and evaluation details are given in Appendix A . Baselines and variants. We compare against vanilla sampled reverse-KL OPD, SuRe ( Shao et al., 2026 ) , and PowerOPD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We implement SuRe within our framework and evaluate it under the same unified training setup as our methods. For PowerOPD, we evaluate both the unified and official reference configurations and report the better result for each teacher–student setting to ensure a fair and conservative comparison. Implementation details and results for both configurations are provided in Appendix A.4 . Among our methods, GC-OPD serves as a diagnostic control that removes the explicit 1 − p S 1-p_{\mathrm{S}} suppression while retaining the log-ratio signal, whereas Bernoulli OPD is our primary proposed objective. We additionally study Balanced Bernoulli OPD and a scale-matched Bernoulli control in Section 5.3 to examine confidence-level rebalancing and the effect of overall optimization magnitude. 5.2 Main Results Table 2 summarizes the main results across four teacher–student settings. Bernoulli OPD improves aggregate reasoning performance over vanilla OPD in all four settings, with gains ranging from 0.98 0.98 to 7.38 7.38 points. The largest improvement occurs in our primary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B setting, where Bernoulli OPD increases the five-benchmark average from 44.38 44.38 to 51.76 51.76 . The improvement also persists with the Qwen3-8B-DAPO-RL teacher and across both settings using the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B student, indicating that the benefit is not specific to a single student or teacher family. The existing baselines show different strengths across settings. SuRe modifies the confidence preference of sampled OPD, while PowerOPD uses a bounded transformation of the log-ratio reward and provides a strong competitive baseline. Bernoulli OPD achieves the highest aggregate performance across all four settings. GC-OPD also improves over vanilla OPD in every setting, providing evidence that reducing the confidence-dependent suppression of sampled reverse KL can be beneficial. Bernoulli OPD further improves over GC-OPD across all four settings. One possible explanation is that Bernoulli OPD not only removes the additional suppression of high-confidence tokens, but also expresses teacher–student disagreement directly through a Bernoulli cross-entropy objective with a bounded sampled-token logit gradient. This combination may provide a more effective training signal across different teacher–student settings. The magnitude of the Bernoulli OPD improvement nevertheless varies substantially across teachers. This suggests that correcting gradient allocation determines which teacher corrections can act strongly on the student, but does not by itself determine how useful those corrections are. We further analyze this teacher-dependent variation in Sec. 5.4 . Figure 4 : Confidence redistribution after OPD training. Changes in token share across confidence bins relative to the initial student under (a) fixed-rollout rescoring and (b) on-policy generation. Bernoulli OPD shows the strongest redistribution away from the highest-confidence region. 5.3 Additional Variants for Bernoulli OPD We further examine two questions: (1) does making the gradient allocation more uniform across confidence regions improve performance? (2) are the gains of Bernoulli OPD simply due to a larger overall optimization step? Balanced Bernoulli OPD. Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens, but it does not explicitly attempt to equalize gradient mass across confidence regions. Its gradient magnitude remains determined by the underlying teacher–student probability discrepancy, | p S − p T | |p_{S}-p_{T}| , which can itself vary substantially with student confidence. This raises a natural question: once the severe suppression of high-confidence tokens is removed, would making the gradient allocation even more balanced across confidence regions lead to further gains? To examine this question, we introduce Balanced Bernoulli OPD as a diagnostic extension that explicitly reweights Bernoulli updates according to the aggregate gradient mass in each confidence region. Specifically, we partition valid response tokens into B B bins according to their student probability p S p_{S} . For each bin b b , we compute its aggregate Bernoulli gradient mass M b = ∑ t ∈ b | p S ​ ( t ) − p T ​ ( t ) | . M_{b}=\sum_{t\in b}\left|p_{S}(t)-p_{T}(t)\right|. (12) Let M ¯ \bar{M} denote the mean mass across valid bins. We assign tokens in bin b b a detached weight w ~ b = ( M ¯ M b + ϵ ) β , \tilde{w}_{b}=\left(\frac{\bar{M}}{M_{b}+\epsilon}\right)^{\beta}, (13) followed by normalization over valid tokens and clipping to limit extreme weights. By construction, Balanced Bernoulli pushes the gradient allocation toward a more even distribution across student-confidence regions than standard Bernoulli OPD. If the remaining imbalance under Bernoulli OPD were itself an important limitation, this stronger rebalancing should provide additional downstream benefit. Table 3 , however, shows no such consistent improvement. Balanced Bernoulli yields only small gains of 0.11 0.11 , 0.27 0.27 , and 0.06 0.06 points in three settings, while decreasing the five-benchmark average by 0.92 0.92 points with the Skywork-OR1-Math-7B teacher. Rather, the main benefit comes from removing the strong objective-induced suppression of high-confidence tokens while allowing the remaining gradient distribution to reflect the natural teacher–student probability discrepancies present in the data. The gradient allocation induced directly by Bernoulli OPD therefore appears sufficient: explicitly flattening it further provides little additional benefit and can even be detrimental. We consequently use standard Bernoulli OPD as our primary objective and treat Balanced Bernoulli OPD only as a mechanism control. Gradient-scale control. Figure 3 shows that Bernoulli OPD produces a substantially different gradient profile from vanilla OPD, raising the possibility that its gain results simply from a larger overall update. To isolate this effect, we construct a scale-matched Bernoulli variant whose loss is rescaled at initialization to match the full-model gradient norm of vanilla OPD. Table 4 summarizes the result. Scale matching makes both the initial gradient norm and one-step policy movement nearly identical to vanilla OPD while preserving Bernoulli OPD’s distinct confidence-dependent gradient allocation. The downstream advantage also remains: scale-matched Bernoulli reaches an average accuracy of 52.58 52.58 , compared with 44.38 44.38 for vanilla OPD and 51.76 51.76 for standard Bernoulli OPD. In this diagnostic setting, the gain therefore cannot be explained solely by a larger global update. We next examine how different OPD objectives affect the confidence distribution of the trained student. Figure 4 reports the change in token share across confidence bins relative to the initial student. This suggests that its performance gain cannot be explained solely by generating longer responses, but reflects a different learning trajectory induced by the objective. 6 Conclusion We show that sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, even though these tokens can still provide useful learning signal. We introduce Bernoulli OPD, which replaces the log-ratio surrogate with a Bernoulli cross-entropy objective whose sampled-token logit gradient directly reflects the bounded teacher–student probability difference. Across four teacher–student settings, Bernoulli OPD consistently improves over vanilla OPD. Our controls further show that the gain is not explained simply by a larger update or by enforcing more uniform gradients across confidence regions. Overall, our results highlight the importance of separating token informativeness from the gradient geometry of the distillation objective.
